messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omar is a 22-year-old auditor who had been in his first serious relationship when he was raped by his ex-boyfriend after an evening at the other man’s apartment. He remembers the scene in concrete sensory fragments: the heavy scent of his ex’s cologne mixed with sweat, the abrupt movement when his ex blocked the doorway, the shock of hearing familiar words spoken in a tone that made refusal feel pointless. What continues to disturb Omar is not only the assault itself but the sense that something deeply wrong and degrading was done to him by someone he had trusted. Since then, phrases that sound like the way his ex used to speak to him can make his stomach drop, and when he encounters a similar smell on a crowded elevator or in the hallway outside a client meeting, he feels thrown back into that night and flooded with humiliation.

In the weeks afterward, Omar became preoccupied with what the assault said about him. He had come to believe that somebody stronger, smarter, or less naive would not have gotten into that situation. He compares himself constantly to an imagined other man who would have seen the danger sooner, left earlier, fought harder. Alongside that self-comparison is a more global loss: he describes himself as having once been easygoing and upbeat, and now feeling persistently miserable, as if that version of himself has been replaced by someone smaller and ashamed. Encounters that remind him of his ex, or even seeing people behave in ways he experiences as selfish, boundary-violating, or morally wrong, do not simply upset him; they revive the conviction that he has been permanently humiliated.

That belief has shaped how he moves through the world. At work, where he spends long hours in conference rooms with clients and senior staff reviewing financial discrepancies, he is acutely aware of being observed. He avoids situations in which his appearance or performance might be scrutinized more than necessary, speaking less in meetings when he can, dreading presentations, and choosing loose, concealing clothing that makes him feel less exposed. He often seats himself near the door in audit meetings or training sessions so he can leave quickly if he starts to feel trapped. The logic makes immediate sense to him: if being noticed is dangerous and if he has already shown himself to be the kind of person to end up degraded, then minimizing visibility feels like the only way to protect himself.

Over time his body has come to operate as if danger is always close. Omar describes himself as constantly tense, with his shoulders tight and his attention scanning the room before he can settle. Sudden movements from other people—someone reaching across a table too quickly, a coworker stepping behind him unexpectedly—put him instantly on guard. Because unfamiliar places feel impossible to assess, he avoids them whenever he can, preferring known routes, known coffee shops, known office spaces. That persistent sense of threat feeds directly into his habits of protection: he checks where the exits are almost automatically, declines invitations to new venues after work, and chooses seats that keep other people in view.

The habits that were meant to make him safer have narrowed his life and seem to keep the problem alive. By sticking to the edges of rooms and dressing to disappear, he remains intensely focused on whether anyone is noticing him, whether someone is moving too close, whether a smell in the air resembles his ex’s cologne. The more he scans, the more readily those reminders seem to appear. A client’s aftershave, a stranger’s sudden gesture, or a joking phrase that echoes his ex can set off the same jolt. When that happens and he slips out early or avoids the next situation entirely, he is left feeling even more different from other people and more convinced that the assault has marked him in a lasting way. In his mind, the precautions also become evidence: if he has to live like this, he tells himself, then maybe he really is damaged and permanently diminished.

This has begun to affect his work and his relationships. He remains competent as an auditor, but he has started turning down opportunities that would place him in unfamiliar offices or require more visible performance. He stays single and keeps interactions carefully bounded. What finally brought him to treatment was the realization that his world had become organized around escape routes, vigilance, and avoidance, and that even routine workdays could be derailed by a smell in an elevator or a comment that sounded too much like his ex. What frightens Omar most is that he may never stop feeling humiliated and on guard. What he hopes, more quietly, is that he might recover some sense of safety without having to disappear.
